documents.unit: Division of Information Technology (AI resources for teaching)
documents.title: Developing an AI Use Statement (Syllabus Statements)
tiers: AI Use Permitted for Individual Assignments
AI Use Permitted for Specific Purposes
AI Use Generally Permitted with Attribution or Disclosure
documents.summary: University IT page telling instructors to write their own AI syllabus statement, because the integrity policy has no AI clause. It supplies five sample statements ranging from a full ban to general permission with attribution.
documents.stance_why: The page says the integrity policy has no separate clause on AI and that "instructors should ... add a statement to syllabi", then offers five templates from a ban to general permission, so the university sets no stance and hands the decision to instructors with tiers.

units.why: The page states a fact about the University's own policy: "do not include a separate clause on the use of AI tools". It is an admin-level statement of the policy gap; no listed type covers it, so it is UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: do not include a separate clause
units.uncovered_note: States that the university's academic-integrity policy has no AI-specific clause, which is why the decision falls to instructors.

units.why: "instructors should ... add a statement to syllabi" is a recommendation to instructors to put AI expectations in the syllabus, which is P09 (syllabus statement). Modality is should, not must.
units.anchor: add a statement to syllabi clearly addressing the restrictions or appropriate uses of AI

units.why: The list of considerations for a course AI policy begins with "Alignment with learning goals", i.e. AI decisions should follow from learning objectives (P83).
units.anchor: Alignment with learning goals
units.policy: When crafting a course AI policy, instructors take into account alignment with learning goals.

units.why: Second listed consideration for a course AI policy: "Equity and access for all students", which matches P51 (equity and access).
units.anchor: Equity and access for all students
units.policy: When crafting a course AI policy, instructors take into account equity and access for all students.

units.why: Third listed consideration: "Information security and data privacy", matching P50 (protect data).
units.anchor: Information security and data privacy
units.policy: When crafting a course AI policy, instructors take into account information security and data privacy.

units.why: Fourth listed consideration: "Copyright and academic integrity". Copyright is the more specific content so P52 is chosen; academic integrity has no separate type here.
units.anchor: Copyright and academic integrity
units.policy: When crafting a course AI policy, instructors take into account copyright and academic integrity.
units.fit_note: Also names academic integrity, which P52 does not capture.

units.why: The page offers five sample statements "reflect[ing] varied stances" that instructors may revise; this is a template menu of tiers of AI use, so P05.
units.anchor: reflect varied stances on using AI in courses and can be revised as needed
units.policy: The five example statements reflect varied stances on using AI in courses and can be revised as needed.

units.why: Names the working group from which the sample statements were adapted, describing how the guidance was produced; P84 covers provenance of policy text.
units.anchor: adapted from the Teachers College AI and Pedagogy Working Group
units.policy: The example statements are adapted from the Teachers College AI and Pedagogy Working Group.

units.why: Example 1 says "Students are prohibited from using Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools" for coursework, a default ban on graded work (P01).
units.anchor: Students are prohibited from using Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools to complete coursework

units.why: "Violation ... will be considered academic dishonesty" classifies misuse as misconduct handled by integrity procedures (P36).
units.anchor: Violation of this policy will be considered academic dishonesty

units.why: Students with an "AI accommodation" are told to speak to the instructor, an accommodation provision. P51 includes accommodations and alternatives; P97 is about tool output, so P51 fits better.
units.anchor: registered with DSS with an AI accommodation, please speak with me directly
units.policy: Students registered with DSS who have an AI accommodation speak with the instructor directly about their needs.

units.why: Example 2 sets AI permission assignment by assignment: "Each assignment will specify whether AI can be used". That is P04 (per-assignment rule).
units.anchor: Each assignment will specify whether AI can be used and how it should be utilized.

units.why: Puts the burden on students to read and follow each assignment's AI guidelines: P78 (learn and follow each course's rules).
units.anchor: Students are responsible for carefully reading and following these guidelines.

units.why: "citations detailing the specific AI tools and models" requires tool/model-specific citation, P25 rather than the general P24.
units.anchor: Proper citations detailing the specific AI tools and models used must be included.

units.why: "Unauthorized use of AI tools will be considered academic dishonesty" is P36; the trigger (unauthorized use) differs from Example 1's, so it is coded separately.
units.anchor: Unauthorized use of AI tools will be considered academic dishonesty

units.why: Example 3 lists permitted uses; finding background information is search-engine-like help to understand a topic (P12).
units.anchor: Helping you find background information about a topic
units.policy: AI tools may be used for helping students find background information about a topic.

units.why: Permitted use: "summaries or explanations of challenging material for your own reflection", AI as a tutor for understanding (P12). P14 (study aids) is close but explanation of material is the core.
units.anchor: Generating summaries or explanations of challenging material
units.policy: AI tools may be used for generating summaries or explanations of challenging material for the student's own reflection.

units.why: Permitted use "Drafting outlines to help you organize your thoughts" is writing support (P91).
units.anchor: Drafting outlines to help you organize your thoughts
units.policy: AI tools may be used for drafting outlines to help students organize their thoughts.

units.why: Permitted use "Improving grammar and style" is editing support (P91).
units.anchor: Improving grammar and style
units.policy: AI tools may be used for improving grammar and style.

units.why: Under "may NOT be used for any other purposes, including" the example bans drafting writing assignments, i.e. having AI produce submitted text (P19).
units.anchor: Drafting writing assignments
units.policy: AI tools may not be used for drafting writing assignments.

units.why: The same list bans using AI for "Analyzing data". No type captures a ban on AI data analysis (P89 is the permission), so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Analyzing data
units.policy: AI tools may not be used for analyzing data.
units.uncovered_note: A specific prohibition on using AI to analyze data; P89 covers only the permitting side.

units.why: "permitted only for the specific tasks listed" is a whitelist: banned unless listed, a narrow-list restriction. Nearest is P05 (named categories of use).
units.anchor: permitted only for the specific tasks listed above
units.fit_note: A whitelist rule: any use outside the listed tasks is not allowed; P05 covers naming categories but not the closed-list restriction.

units.why: Requires citation of tool, model and "how they were utilized", which goes beyond tool name to describe use (P25).
units.anchor: citations detailing the specific AI tools and models used and how they were utilized

units.why: Example 4 conditions all AI use on "explicit approval from the instructor": a restrict stance that sends each case to the instructor (P04).
units.anchor: only after obtaining explicit approval from the instructor
units.fit_note: Per-use prior instructor approval; P04 does not capture the approval-before-use gate.

units.why: Students must file a written proposal before using AI. No type covers a proposal-and-approval procedure, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: students must submit a brief written proposal outlining how the AI tool will be used
units.uncovered_note: A procedure requiring a written proposal stating how and why AI will be used, submitted before use.

units.why: States the criteria instructors use to approve AI proposals: "appropriateness and educational value". Not covered by a type; UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Approval will be granted based on the appropriateness and educational value
units.uncovered_note: Criteria for approving a student's proposed AI use: appropriateness and educational value.

units.why: Example 5: AI "generally allowed ... for research and assignment completion" with attribution, a permit-by-default stance (P02).
units.anchor: generally allowed in this course for research and assignment completion

units.why: Condition on permission: "all AI-generated content is clearly attributed", a disclosure duty (P24).
units.anchor: all AI-generated content is clearly attributed in the student’s work

units.why: Makes non-attribution itself the violation, which is P28 (nondisclosure is the violation).
units.anchor: Failure to properly attribute AI-assisted work will be considered academic dishonesty

documents.title: Mitigate AI-Generated Content
documents.summary: Faculty guidance listing assignment designs to reduce AI-generated work and a list of AI-detection tools with caveats. It sets no student rule.
documents.stance_why: The page gives "recommendations for adapting course assignments" and says AI "may not be appropriate for use by all disciplines", without any rule for students; the decision rests with instructors, so delegates.

units.why: The page says AI "may not be appropriate for use by all disciplines", leaving fit to discipline and instructor. Nearest is P04; the discipline-level point is not captured exactly.
units.anchor: the use of AI may not be appropriate for use by all disciplines
units.fit_note: Appropriateness of AI is said to vary by discipline rather than by instructor or assignment.

units.why: Acknowledges that GenAI "provide[s] opportunities for its integration into the classroom", a general statement of benefit without a rule (P87).
units.anchor: advances in GenAI provide opportunities for its integration into the classroom

units.why: The page frames its guidance as "recommendations for adapting course assignments and activities to reduce the use of AI-generated content", i.e. redesign assignments around AI (P35).
units.anchor: recommendations for adapting course assignments and activities to reduce the use of AI-generated content

units.why: Under the heading "Real-World Application" instructors are advised to change assignment design so AI output is less useful ("Craft assignments that require students to apply course concepts to real-world scenarios"), which is assignment redesign (P35).
units.anchor: Craft assignments that require students to apply course concepts to real-world scenarios

units.why: Under the heading "Case Studies" instructors are advised to change assignment design so AI output is less useful ("Assign case studies or specific examples that are not readily available"), which is assignment redesign (P35).
units.anchor: Assign case studies or specific examples that are not readily available

units.why: Under the heading "Original Research" instructors are advised to change assignment design so AI output is less useful ("Encourage students to conduct original research or experiments."), which is assignment redesign (P35).
units.anchor: Encourage students to conduct original research or experiments.

units.why: Under the heading "Experiential Learning" instructors are advised to change assignment design so AI output is less useful ("Create assignments that involve experiential learning"), which is assignment redesign (P35).
units.anchor: Create assignments that involve experiential learning

units.why: Under the heading "Group Projects" instructors are advised to change assignment design so AI output is less useful ("Assign collaborative projects that require students to work together"), which is assignment redesign (P35).
units.anchor: Assign collaborative projects that require students to work together

units.why: Under the heading "Reflection and Analysis" instructors are advised to change assignment design so AI output is less useful ("Ask students to reflect on their personal experiences, goals, or the course content."), which is assignment redesign (P35).
units.anchor: Ask students to reflect on their personal experiences, goals, or the course content.

units.why: Under the heading "Creative Assignments" instructors are advised to change assignment design so AI output is less useful ("Assign creative projects such as art, music, writing, or design tasks"), which is assignment redesign (P35).
units.anchor: Assign creative projects such as art, music, writing, or design tasks

units.why: Under the heading "Class Discussions and Debates" instructors are advised to change assignment design so AI output is less useful ("Incorporate assignments that involve participation in class discussions, debates, or forums."), which is assignment redesign (P35).
units.anchor: Incorporate assignments that involve participation in class discussions, debates, or forums.

units.why: Under the heading "Peer Reviews" instructors are advised to change assignment design so AI output is less useful ("Implement peer review processes where students evaluate and provide feedback"), which is assignment redesign (P35).
units.anchor: Implement peer review processes where students evaluate and provide feedback

units.why: Under the heading "Open-Ended Questions" instructors are advised to change assignment design so AI output is less useful ("Frame assignments with open-ended questions"), which is assignment redesign (P35).
units.anchor: Frame assignments with open-ended questions

units.why: Under the heading "Continuous Assessment" instructors are advised to change assignment design so AI output is less useful ("Break assignments into smaller, incremental tasks with checkpoints along the way."), which is assignment redesign (P35).
units.anchor: Break assignments into smaller, incremental tasks with checkpoints along the way.

units.why: Under the heading "Citation and Source Analysis" instructors are advised to change assignment design so AI output is less useful ("Include assignments that focus on evaluating sources, analyzing their credibility"), which is assignment redesign (P35).
units.anchor: Include assignments that focus on evaluating sources, analyzing their credibility

units.why: Under the heading "Individualized Assignments" instructors are advised to change assignment design so AI output is less useful ("Customize assignments to the individual needs and interests of each student"), which is assignment redesign (P35).
units.anchor: Customize assignments to the individual needs and interests of each student

units.why: Under the heading "Authentic Assessment" instructors are advised to change assignment design so AI output is less useful ("Align assignments with real-world scenarios"), which is assignment redesign (P35).
units.anchor: Align assignments with real-world scenarios

units.why: An in-class writing task gives "a baseline writing sample" to compare later work; P35 names baselines as an example of redesign. P33 (proctored assessment) also touches it but the point is the baseline for comparison.
units.anchor: This will provide faculty with a baseline writing sample
units.policy: Faculty ask students for an in-class writing assignment through Honorlock to provide a baseline writing sample to compare future work against.

units.why: Advises timed and in-class assessment to limit access to AI, shifting weight to unassisted evaluation (P33).
units.anchor: Use timed quizzes, tests, or in-class writing assignments to reduce the opportunity

units.why: Oral presentations let students "demonstrate their understanding", a way to check understanding through explanation (P34).
units.anchor: Assign presentations or speeches that require students to communicate verbally

units.why: In-class assessment with "limited access" to AI is unassisted assessment (P33).
units.anchor: Conduct assessments during class time, where students have limited access

units.why: Says faculty "can leverage Honorlock to proctor" in-class assessments, a proctoring option for unassisted work (P33).
units.anchor: Faculty can leverage Honorlock to proctor the assignment.

units.why: "False positives and negatives may happen" and modified text is "difficult to detect": the limits of detectors (P39). The page still lists detectors, so the fit is partial.
units.anchor: False positives and negatives may happen.
units.fit_note: Admits detector unreliability but does not say detectors should not be used; the page goes on to recommend several.

units.why: Tells instructors to understand how a detector works and read its reports. No type covers detector literacy, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: know how the AI detection tool works and understand the reports
units.uncovered_note: Instructors should understand how an AI-detection tool works and how to read its reports.

units.why: States that AI output will become "harder to detect", a limit on verifying originality (P82).
units.anchor: As AI tools evolve, they will become harder to detect.

units.why: Recommends starting with an "in-class and/or proctored writing assignment" as a sample of original writing: a baseline-sample redesign step (P35).
units.anchor: start with an in-class and/or proctored writing assignment for a sample of original writing

units.why: Names Turnitin as the university's checker that estimates human versus AI-generated writing: a similarity/detection tool for identifying misuse (P40).
units.anchor: Turnitin is the University’s plagiarism checker within Canvas.

units.why: Lists GPTZero as a detector for checking whether a document was written by an LLM (P40).
units.anchor: GPTZero is the leading AI detector for checking whether a document was written

units.why: States GPTZero's limit: "not trained to identify AI-generated text after it has been heavily modified". A statement of detector limits (P39).
units.anchor: not trained to identify AI-generated text after it has been heavily modified
units.fit_note: Describes one tool's limitation, not a rule against reliance.

units.why: Lists Content at Scale as a detector and repeats a vendor accuracy claim ("98% accuracy"), a detection tool offered for use (P40).
units.anchor: Content at Scale is an AI Detector

units.why: Lists Writefull's detector as an option to identify AI-written content (P40).
units.anchor: Writefull GPT Detector can identify content written by GPT-3

units.why: Lists Hive's detector for text and images (P40).
units.anchor: Hive AI Detector can be used for both text and image detection.

documents.title: Ethical Considerations and Limitations
documents.summary: Short faculty-facing page on AI risks: integrity, bias, misinformation, data privacy and accessibility. It advises instructors to address expectations before integrating AI.
documents.stance_why: It says to "consider the implications and limitations" "before making any determinations about if and how to integrate AI" and offers advice only, so no stance is set and delegates fits.

units.why: Names the benefit of AI as a "personalized learning experience", no rule attached (P87).
units.anchor: create a personalized learning experience for each student

units.why: Advises instructors to weigh implications and limitations before deciding on AI, i.e. learn the implications before setting policy (P63).
units.anchor: Before making any determinations about if and how to integrate AI into teaching and learning
units.fit_note: Advice to consider implications before deciding; no workshops or support are mentioned.

units.why: Says suitability varies by discipline, so the rule is left to the teaching context (P04).
units.anchor: Some disciplines are more suited for using AI/Gen AI than others.
units.fit_note: Variation is by discipline, not instructor or assignment.

units.why: Instructors are told to add a self-paced module to the syllabus to educate students on integrity and plagiarism: a training module for students (P70). It is about integrity generally, not AI.
units.anchor: Adding the self-paced Academic Integrity Module to your syllabus
units.fit_note: The module teaches the Academic Integrity Policy and plagiarism, not AI specifically.

units.why: Instructors are advised to discuss the ethics and limits of AI with students, going beyond listing a rule (P66).
units.anchor: Discussing the ethical considerations and limitations of using AI/Gen AI.

units.why: Advises having students "sign an honor code or statement of understanding". No type covers signed pledges, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Have students sign an honor code or statement of understanding.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors have students sign an honor code or statement of understanding about AI use.

units.why: Advises using "plagiarism and AI-generated content detection tools" to identify dishonesty (P40).
units.anchor: Utilizing plagiarism and AI-generated content detection tools to help identify instances

units.why: States that models "inherit biases" and may perpetuate discrimination: bias concerns (P53).
units.anchor: Generative AI models can inherit biases present in their training data

units.why: "essential to critically analyze the results" and compare with other sources is a duty to verify AI output (P31).
units.anchor: it is essential to critically analyze the results it provides

units.why: Users must understand "potential for inaccuracies" (hallucination) and learn to derive facts: verify AI output (P31).
units.anchor: understand the potential for inaccuracies in AI-generated content

units.why: "responsibility of ... faculty, staff and students to safeguard confidential information" is a data-protection duty for everyone (P50).
units.anchor: responsibility of Seton Hall faculty, staff and students to safeguard confidential information

units.why: Warns that sharing confidential data with third-party AI "may expose that data"; a privacy warning (P50).
units.anchor: sharing sensitive or confidential information with third-party AI tools may expose that data

units.why: Requires adherence to the existing "data security policy", compliance with existing university policy (P77).
units.anchor: must adhere to the University’s data security policy

units.why: Institutions "should ensure that AI systems are compliant with accessibility standards": accessibility of AI tools (P97).
units.anchor: Institutions should ensure that AI systems are compliant with accessibility standards

units.why: A separate duty in the same sentence: AI systems must not "disadvantage certain groups of students", an equity concern (P51).
units.anchor: do not inadvertently disadvantage certain groups of students
units.fit_note: Fairness across student groups rather than cost or access.

notes: Excluded seton-hall-aiac (screen=exclude) not coded. No computing or school documents found. The university-level pages are IT-division faculty guidance, not a formal policy; the integrity policy AI clause named in the collect notes was not located. List items on the Mitigating page were coded one unit each as separate recommendations.
